title: Going beyond Quietness: Determining the Emotionally Restorative Effect of Acoustic Environments in Urban Open Public Spaces
research_question: To determine the influence of the sound environment and its perception (soundscape) in urban open public spaces on users' health, specifically measuring effects on positive and negative emotional states and perceived stress, and identifying soundscape characteristics that enhance emotional restoration and reduce perceived stress.

participants.description: Residents of Vitoria-Gasteiz, Spain. Mean age 42.3 years (SD = 14.18), range 19-75. 54% women, 46% men. 46.4% university education, 39.0% secondary education. 40.4% employed, 16.9% unemployed. Participants made 137 observations in total.
participants.recruitment: Recruited through civic associations in Vitoria-Gasteiz, Spain. Participation was voluntary.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four urban open public spaces in Vitoria-Gasteiz, Spain, selected for diverse characteristics in natural elements and function: Los Herrán (greyest, high traffic), Constitución (grey, near city entrance), Salinillas (green, sparse vegetation, near green belt), Olarizu (greenest, water, part of city's green belt). Characterized by maintenance, safety, shops, traffic, facilities, trees, water, landmarks, heritage, % green, % blue, % sky, % grey.

measures.instrument: Semantic differential (SD) scale (13 bipolar adjectives, 5-point ordinal scale): pleasant, calm, relaxing, uninterrupted, familiar, facilitates conversation, informative, clear, characteristic, lively (vibrant), fun, natural, appropriate-surroundings
Semantic differential (SD) scale (3 items, 5-point ordinal scale): pleasantness, quietness, naturalness
Smartphone with external microphone (LAeq,mean, LAmax, LAmin, No. total events, No. positive events, No. negative events)
Expert assessment (0-3 or 0-2 scale): Maintenance, Safety, Shops, Traffic, Facilities, Trees, Water, Landmarks, Heritage, % green, % blue, % sky, % grey

mechanisms: Psychological restoration: Urban environmental experiences can reduce negative emotions and perceived stress, and slightly increase positive emotions.
Environmental comfort: Holistic environmental comfort (including acoustic comfort) is strongly associated with better emotional states and reduced stress.
Soundscape characteristics: Pleasantness, calm, fun, and naturalness in the soundscape contribute to greater emotional restoration and stress reduction.
Prior emotional states: Baseline emotional states significantly predict post-experience emotional states.
implementation_implications: Urban design should incorporate soundscape planning to promote psychological restoration, not just quietness.
Enhancing natural components (e.g., encouraging insects, birds, wind-plant interaction, water sounds) in urban spaces can improve emotional well-being.
Collaboration between urban designers and acoustics experts is crucial from early project stages.
Urban furniture can be designed to enhance soundscape perception.

limitations: The study duration was short, which may have limited the detection of statistically significant changes in positive emotions.
The beneficial effect on positive emotions may be more strongly associated with naturalness, which is harder to find in urban environments.
The method (smartphone application) proved somewhat complex and might have limitations compared to laboratory studies.
The study sample size and diversity of urban spaces considered were limited.
The experiment itself or the attention participants received might have contributed to emotional restoration.
The influence of the length of time of the test should be investigated in greater depth for different restorative effects.
Participants were not asked to identify potential keynote sounds, limiting analysis of their contribution to comfort/restoration.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The capacity of natural settings to promote psychological restoration has attracted increasing research attention, especially with regards to the visual dimension. However, there is a need to extend these studies to urban settings, such as squares, parks or gardens, due to the global trend towards urbanisation, and to integrate the dimension of sound into landscape. Such was the main aim of this study, in which 53 participants assessed four public spaces in Vitoria-Gasteiz (Spain) as part of the CITI-SENSE Project (137 observations were used for analysis). A smartphone application was used to simultaneously collect objective and subjective data. The results show that at the end of the urban environmental experience, there was a statistically significant reduction in negative emotions and perceived stress, and a slight increase in positive emotions. Emotional restoration was mainly associated with prior emotional states, but also with global environmental comfort and acoustic comfort. The soundscape characteristics that contributed to greater emotional restoration and a reduction in perceived stress were pleasantness, calm, fun and naturalness. Therefore, in agreement with previous research, the findings of the present study indicate that besides contributing to the quietness of the urban environment, the urban soundscape can promote psychological restoration in users of these spaces.
